picked.t: IBK기업은행, 9년 공들인 베트남 현지법인 공식 영업 돌입 '중소기업 밀착 지원'
picked.body: 지난 13일 베트남 하노이에서 개최된 'IBK베트남은행 출범식'에서 (왼쪽 여섯 번째부터) 이미연 주베트남 대한민국 대사, 팜꽝중 베트남 중앙은행 부총재, 장민영 IBK기업은행장, 김기문 중소기업중앙회 회장, 고태연 주베트남한국상공인연합회 회장, (맨 오른쪽) 박경일 IBK베트남은행 법인장 등이 기념촬영을 하고 있는 모습 (사진=기업은행) 'IBK베트남은행'이 엄격한 외국계 은행 규제로 유명한 베트남 금융시장의 높은 문턱을 넘어서 첫발을 내딛었다. IBK기업은행은 지난 13일 베트남 수도 하노이에서 현지 법인인 'IBK베트남은행'의 정식 출범 행사를 개최했다고 14일 밝혔다.  IBK기업은행은 지난 4월 베트남 중앙은행(SBV)으로부터 최종 본인가를 획득한 지 수개월 만에 모든 행정·실무 절차를 완료하고, 9월 25일부터 본격적인 영업 활동에 돌입한 상태다. 이번 법인 설립은 베트남 당국의 은행권 구조조정과 외국계 금융사 인가 동결 기조 속에서 달성한 성과다. 기업은행은 장장 9년에 걸쳐 현지 금융당국을 설득한 끝에 베트남 내 10번째 외국계 법인은행 타이틀을 거머쥐었다. 새롭게 닻을 올린 IBK베트남은행은 기존 하노이와 호치민 거점 지점의 운영 실적에 더해, 지난 60여 년간 국내에서 입증된 중소기업 전용 정책금융 시스템을 이식한다.  특히 한국 기업들이 대거 입주한 주요 산업단지를 중심으로 거점 점포를 점진적으로 늘려나갈 계획이다. 이를 통해 현지에 진출한 한국 기업은 물론 현지 중소기업에도 자금을 활발히 공급하는 생산적 금융을 구현하고, 양국의 경제적 연대를 공고히 한다는 전략이다. 박경일 IBK기업은행 초대 법인장은 2008년 호치민 지점으로 시작된 베트남 영토 확장이 이번 법인화로 완성된 현지화의 이정표가 되었다고 평가했다. 이어 비가 올 때 우산을 씌워주는 상생 금융 역량을 바탕으로, 베트남 경제와 궤를 같이하며 성장하는 든든한 파트너 은행으로 뿌리내리겠다는 비전을 밝혔다.

picked.t: From employee to daughter-in-law: Vietnamese woman marries Korean boss's son
picked.body: After years of working directly under her strict Korean boss in Hai Phong, Pham Anh Tho trusted her so deeply that when the woman's son proposed after just three months of dating, she agreed to marry him. Tho, a graduate of Vietnam Maritime University, joined a technology equipment installation company in Hai Phong in 2021 as a safety officer and interpreter. There, she worked directly under Park Soo-jeong, 58, the Korean woman who ran the business. "At work, I was terrified of her because she was strict and disciplined, but outside the office, she was very warm and friendly," Tho recalls. Tho lived in Le Chan District, near the company dormitory. When Park noticed that she often worked late and missed the bus home, she would give her a ride in the company car. Knowing Tho loved kimchi, Park frequently invited her over whenever she cooked Korean food. She also took the young employee grocery shopping, to concerts and on food tours around Hai Phong. "I was fond of her, but I never imagined she would one day become my daughter-in-law," says Park, a Seoul native. In March 2021, Park's son Gil-sun moved to Vietnam to help with the family business. The 1.85-meter-tall Korean man soon noticed Tho, who stood just 1.5 meters tall. "My mother and sister are both tall, so I have always liked petite, cute women," the now 34-year-old says. Tho also noticed him, not least because he was the youngest and tallest among the Korean staff. Gil-sun began buying her snacks and inviting her to dinner, joking that he needed her to act as his tour guide in Hai Phong. Their friendship quickly developed into a romance. Park was pleased when she realized her son was interested in Tho, though she also worried about the challenges of a cross-cultural relationship. "You must be serious about her because she is a good girl," she told him, warning him to be thoughtful and avoid misunderstandings arising from cultural differences. Around two months later, Gil-sun had to return to South Korea. With the Covid-19 pandemic making it unclear when he could come back to Vietnam, he asked his mother to formally approach Tho's family on his behalf and ask for her hand in marriage as proof of his commitment. Tho initially hesitated. But her years of working with Park had given her confidence in the family. She believed that a disciplined woman like Park would have raised her son to be responsible and respectable. Tho's parents in Hai Phong were also skeptical at first. But after meeting Gil-sun and seeing his modesty and sincerity, they gave the couple their blessing. Their wedding was held simply during the pandemic. Park personally carried a ceremonial tray to Tho's home as part of the traditional marriage proposal. After the wedding, Tho moved to Seoul to live with her husband's family. There, however, she encountered a way of life very different from the one she had grown up with. Gil-sun's paternal family came from an old aristocratic lineage and placed strong emphasis on tradition and etiquette. Park herself had lived under similarly strict expectations when she was a young daughter-in-law. While her own mother-in-law was alive, she was expected to prepare three meals a day, make late-night snacks and keep the house immaculate regardless of how busy she was. Those habits stayed with her. She expected Tho to wake up early, prepare breakfast and other meals, maintain a tidy home and observe proper forms of respect when speaking to her and her husband. Tho, by contrast, had been pampered by her parents and grew up in a relatively carefree household. She enjoyed going out for coffee, walking around town and eating out with her husband. Adjusting to the rigid household routine in Seoul proved difficult. Small conflicts gradually emerged over meals, everyday habits and later parenting. When disagreements arose, Tho often asked her husband to explain her perspective to his mother, but Gil-sun's clumsy attempts at mediation sometimes made matters worse. "In the beginning, I felt trapped because I was not used to that kind of lifestyle," Tho says. Her sister-in-law eventually became an important ally. As a daughter-in-law herself, she helped Park understand how difficult the transition was for Tho. Over time, Park began to relax her expectations. "I realized it was not that Tho was unwilling to be a good daughter-in-law. I was simply being too strict," she says. "Because I had spent so many years living that way myself, I assumed everyone should do the same." Tho also made an effort to bridge the gap. Instead of avoiding difficult conversations, she began speaking openly with Park. Knowing her mother-in-law enjoyed Vietnamese food, particularly bun dau mam tom—rice vermicelli served with fried tofu and shrimp paste—and northern Vietnamese dishes, she cooked them for her. picked.t: JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi wins multiple international hospitality awards
picked.body: BodyJW Marriott Hotel Hanoi wins multiple international hospitality awards JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi has received several international awards in 2026 for its accommodation, spa and dining services. The hotel has been named one of the six best hotels in Southeast Asia in the 2026 Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards. The annual awards are based on ratings and experiences submitted by travelers worldwide. The hotel also received "Vietnam's Best Golf Hotel 2026" at the Vietnam Golf & Leisure Awards. Its Spa L'Occitane en Provence was named "Vietnam's Best Hotel Spa" at the World Spa Awards 2026 in late September. The hotel's dining venues also received recognition. French Grill was included in the Michelin Selected 2026 list for the fourth consecutive year. French Grill and Kumihimo also received Tripadvisor's 2026 Travelers' Choice Awards Best of the Best. The distinction is awarded to establishments ranked among the top 1% of listings on the platform based on traveler reviews and ratings. A hotel representative attributed the awards to continued investment in facilities, services and staff development. The hotel offers accommodation, meeting facilities, restaurants and wellness experiences for business and leisure travelers. "These achievements across multiple categories not only reinforce JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi's position as a leading luxury destination in the capital but also enhance the appeal of Vietnam's hospitality industry among international travelers," the hotel representative said.

picked.t: Singapore lender UOB raises Vietnam’s growth forecast to 9.2%
picked.body: The United Overseas Bank lifted its 2026 growth forecast for Vietnam from 8.5% in its latest report after the General Statistics Office announced third-quarter GDP growth of 9.95%. The growth was the fastest since the third quarter of 2022 and above the 9% forecasts from both the bank and Bloomberg. The result brought GDP growth in the first nine months to 9.01%, keeping Vietnam the fastest-growing economy in ASEAN. According to UOB, one of Singapore’s largest banks by total assets, manufacturing and investment were the main growth drivers. Industry and construction expanded by 11.21% in the first nine months, accounting for 49.62% of the increase in the economy’s total value added, a larger contribution than services. Electronics remained a pillar of growth, with exports of computers, electronic products and components reaching around US$111 billion by mid-September, reflecting the sector’s growing gains, according to UOB. The bank described the investment outlook as "exceptionally strong" after disbursed foreign direct investment recorded its strongest growth in five years. It expects fourth-quarter growth of around 9.7%, supported by faster public investment disbursement toward year-end. UOB’s forecast is currently among the most optimistic from international institutions, alongside Standard Chartered’s. Over the past two months, the Asian Development Bank and World Bank raised their forecasts for Vietnam’s economic growth to 7.8% and 7.4%, respectively. The government said earlier that GDP must grow by 12.5% in the fourth quarter to achieve the full-year target of 10%. Local authorities have been instructed to closely follow growth scenarios for the final three months, review each growth driver and project, and remove obstacles to production and business operations. Public investment remains a key growth driver, with authorities required to disburse 100% of planned funding. Despite the positive outlook, UOB flagged challenges to monitor, including rising energy prices as the conflict involving Iran remains unresolved and the possibility of stricter U.S. tariffs after next month’s midterm elections. The U.S. Federal Reserve is expected to continue raising interest rates, adding pressure as inflation has exceeded 4.5%, credit growth is outpacing deposit growth, and economic growth is approaching double digits. However, monetary tightening may have limited effectiveness because inflationary pressures largely stem from the supply side, and it risks weakening growth momentum. UOB expects the State Bank of Vietnam to keep its refinancing rate unchanged at 4.5% through the end of 2027 while using open market operations and credit growth limits to manage liquidity. In the foreign exchange market, a return to a trade surplus in the latest month, record FDI inflows and GDP growth above 9% will continue to support the stability of the Vietnamese dong, according to UOB.

picked.t: Russian woman gives up city life to care for mother-in-law in rural Vietnam
picked.body: By 5 a.m. one morning in early October, Elena had already returned from the market to her home in Chan Lac Village, Yen Trung Commune, Bac Ninh Province. She placed fresh vegetables and fish on the kitchen table and began preparing breakfast. After cooking, she went to her 74-year-old mother-in-law’s room to help her wash, change clothes and get ready for the day. The older woman developed dementia after a family tragedy and can no longer care for herself. Elena then took her two children to school by motorbike before returning home to help her husband with his business. It has been her daily routine for nearly two years, since she left Izhevsk, Russia, and settled in Vietnam with her family. "Since moving here, I have come to understand my husband better and see how much responsibility he carries for his family," she says. "I want to share that burden and take care of our own family as well." Elena met Nguyen Ngoc Tung, 45, in 2015 while working near his shop in Russia. They married and had two children, born in 2017 and 2021. For about a decade, the couple built a stable life and family business in Russia and expected to remain there long term, returning to Tung’s hometown only during Tet holidays. That changed in mid-2024, when Tung’s father was killed in a traffic accident and the family returned to Vietnam for the funeral. The shock devastated Tung’s mother. She became increasingly anxious and confused and gradually began losing her memory. Tung is the only son in the family, while his five older sisters are married and have families of their own. "Seeing my husband become thinner from grief broke my heart," Elena recalls. During the 49-day mourning period, Elena watched neighbors regularly come to the house to help prepare offerings and receive visitors. She followed their example, learning how to arrange ceremonial trays and light incense at the family altar. The support of the community, together with her mother-in-law’s worsening condition, prompted Elena to make a life-changing decision: move permanently to Vietnam with her husband and children. The move meant giving up her job, familiar surroundings and urban comforts in Russia to start again in the northern Vietnamese countryside with only limited Vietnamese. At first, even everyday interactions felt unfamiliar. In Russia, Elena had been accustomed to greater personal space and limited interaction with strangers. In the village, however, market vendors often patted her shoulder, touched her cheek and asked personal questions, leaving her confused. After Tung explained that such gestures were simply expressions of friendliness, she gradually became more comfortable and began starting conversations herself. She also learned to cook Vietnamese food with help from one of her sisters-in-law, including nem ran (fried spring rolls), canh ca dua chua (sour fish soup with pickled mustard greens) and thit rang (caramelized pork). "Vietnamese food is so diverse that it took me hours just to distinguish between different spices and herbs," she says. She can now prepare most dishes in a traditional family meal and spends her spare time practicing Vietnamese with her husband. Caring for her mother-in-law, however, remains the biggest challenge. Because Elena still speaks limited Vietnamese, communication between the two is often difficult. She has learned to read the older woman’s facial expressions, eyes and gestures to understand what she needs. Elena feeds her porridge, keeps track of her medication, helps her bathe and massages her arms and legs on cold days. She also encourages her children to spend time talking and playing with their grandmother to keep her spirits up. Tung says he initially worried that the cultural differences and demands of rural life would overwhelm his wife. "My mother’s memory comes and goes, and sometimes she tries to break the locks to get outside," he says. "But my wife has never complained. She always takes care of things so I can focus on work." Elena also keeps track of each family member’s food preferences, her mother-in-law’s medication schedule and her children’s schooling. During the last Lunar New Year, she took charge of preparations as the family’s daughter-in-law, from arranging the New Year’s Eve offering tray to preparing the Tet feast. She and Tung also visited relatives and welcomed guests at home. Though she initially found the busy holiday routine stressful, she gradually came to understand it as an important part of Vietnamese family culture. Last month, Elena’s mother, Natalya, 49, traveled to Vietnam to visit her daughter and her in-laws. Having once worried that Elena might struggle with life in a foreign country, Natalya says she felt reassured after seeing how well her daughter had adapted. The moments she remembers most are the large family meals and afternoon walks through the village with her grandchildren. picked.t: 베트남, 데이터센터 성장 속 ‘전력수요 대응’ 과제 급부상…대규모 인프라 투자 불가피
picked.body: 기사 이해를 돕기위해 AI를 활용해 제작한 이미지입니다. 베트남 데이터센터 시장이 급격한 성장세를 보이고 있는 가운데 급증할 전력 수요에 대응하기 위한 에너지와 인프라 문제가 주요 과제로 급부상하고 있다. 현재 베트남 데이터센터 시장은 정부가 2030년까지 AI(인공지능) 경제를 국내총생산(GDP)의 6%까지 확대할 목표를 세운 뒤 수요가 급격한 증가세를 보이고 있다. 당국에 따르면, 데이터센터 전력 용량은 지난해 약 580MW에서 2030년 980MW 가까이 늘어날 것으로 전망되고 있다. CMC코퍼레이션(CMC Corporation), 비엣텔그룹(Viettel Group) 등 주요 기업에 스마트기술 솔루션을 제공 중인 ABB베트남에 따르면, 데이터센터의 높은 전력 수요는 전력 공급뿐 아니라 전체 송배전 시스템에 부담을 주고 있다. 이 같은 맥락에서 전문가들은 전력 인프라와 기타 기반 인프라가 수요를 따라잡을 만큼 빠르게 확대될 수 있는지가 데이터센터 시장의 지속 가능한 발전을 결정짓는 핵심적 요인이 될 것이라고 지적하고 있다. 향후 대규모 프로젝트 유치 역량은 전기와 전력망, 부지 확보, 연결성 인프라 등에 대한 핵심 인프라의 발전 여부에 달려 있으며, 이 때문에 막대한 투자가 불가피하다는 설명이다. 베트남은 빠르게 성장하는 경제와 데이터센터 같은 신(新)산업 분야 전력 수요에 대응해 2026~2030년 기간 전력 시스템 개발에 약 1,363억 달러를 투자할 계획이다. 전체 투자액에는 발전 1,182억 달러, 송전망 181억 달러가 포함된다. 그러나, 현재 베트남의 전력 공급은 국내 발전원뿐 아니라 수입에도 의존하고 있다. 이에 대해 ABB베트남의 제시카 응우옌(Jessica Nguyen) 대표 겸 이사회 의장·국가책임자는 “전력 시스템 개발은 복잡한 과제”라며 “재생에너지와 수입 전력, 신규 전원 등 공급원 다변화를 통해 안정성을 높이고 특정 공급원에 대한 의존도를 낮추는 것이 장기적인 해법”이라고 설명했다. 그는 이어 “AI와 데이터센터가 직면한 에너지 과제는 베트남에 국한된 특수한 문제가 아니라 전 세계적인 과제”라며 “업계의 지속 가능한 성장 토대를 마련하기 위해 정부와 기업이 협력해 인프라 개발을 앞당겨야 한다”고 강조했다. 한편, 베트남은 명확한 디지털 경제와 AI, 데이터센터 발전 전략 아래 업계의 지속 가능한 발전을 뒷받침할 적절한 정책과 규정과 지원 체계를 마련 해둔 상태다. 응우옌 대표는 "현재의 성장 동력과 정부의 강력한 의지로 볼 때 베트남은 역내 데이터센터 업계의 중요한 거점이 될 유리한 조건을 두루 갖췄다"며 “이러한 맥락에서 베트남은 올바른 방향으로 나아가고 있다”고 평가했다.

picked.t: Vietnamese woman turns California backyard into a slice of the Mekong Delta
picked.body: In late September, Loan and her mother, Nguyen Ngoc, 55, walked into their backyard garden to harvest eggplants, okra, and herbs to prepare bun mam (fermented fish noodle soup). For over a year, the duo have been cooking in an outdoor kitchen built with steel mesh frames and tin roof. Aluminum pans, bamboo trays, and strings of onions and garlic hang on the walls. In the yard, they have put up hammocks and wooden tables and chairs for family gatherings, dining, and admiring the garden. Originally from the Mekong Delta province of Vinh Long, Loan moved to the U.S. in 2013 and took her mother there six years later. Knowing that her mother was accustomed to rural life and loved cooking, Loan and her husband decided to renovate the vacant plot behind their house into a garden. She also wanted her two U.S.-born children to experience her family's traditional lifestyle and culinary culture. The gardening project began in 2020. After hiring professionals to clear the weeds, the couple personally tilled the land, created garden beds, fertilized the soil, and planted trees. Getting seeds was the most time-consuming part. In the case of common fruits and vegetables, Loan bought seeds and saplings from the Vietnamese community in the U.S. But for herbs such as culantro, cilantro, and Thai basil, she had to drive three hours to a Vietnamese market to buy fresh herbs, soak them in water until they rooted, and then plant them in the ground. "Dozens of cuttings died before the plants finally took root, but the thought of not having fresh herbs whenever we want to cook Vietnamese food made us try again," she says. Now, six years after being planted, the garden now boasts dozens of fruit trees like coconut, peach, lemon, plum, jujube, and banana, seasonal fruits, and vegetables like water spinach, tomatoes, sponge gourds, okra, cucumbers, chili peppers, Chinese onions, taro stems, and bitter melons. In early 2025, the couple built an outdoor kitchen to complete their living space. Since local contractors were unfamiliar with the rustic architecture of Southwestern Vietnam, Loan only hired them to erect the iron frame, install the tin roof, and pour the concrete floor. The remaining work, such as running electrical wiring, building wooden shelves, constructing the sink unit, and laying tiles, was done by the couple themselves. Behind the kitchen, her husband planted a row of coconut trees and dug a koi pond, modeled after the one in Loan’s hometown. Cooking utensils such as banh khot (Vietnamese mini savory pancakes) molds, banh xeo (Vietnamese crispy pancakes) pans, bamboo trays, and woven baskets were brought from Vietnam by the family. Since having the outdoor kitchen and garden, Ngoc spends most of her day tending to the trees, making banh xeo, and cooking Mekong Delta-style dishes for her children and grandchildren. "Sitting in the kitchen, listening to the sound of cicadas and birds singing in the garden, I feel like I'm right back in my hometown," she says. On weekends and holidays, the "Mekong Delta-style garden" becomes a gathering spot for the extended family. They harvest vegetables, cook in the kitchen, and lie on the hammocks. Through these outdoor meals, Loan's two children have become familiar with the flavors of bun mam , banh xeo , canh ca bung (eggplant soup), and grilled squid. Whenever she cooks Vietnamese food, she makes extra portions to share with her American neighbors. Many neighbors who come to visit inquire about the design of this open-concept kitchen. In her free time, Loan films her family cooking and harvesting produce, and posts the videos on social media, drawing millions of views. Beneath the videos, many viewers leave comments saying that the tin roof, washing area, and hammock remind them of their homeland. For Loan, the greatest value of the garden is that it helps younger generations stay connected to their roots. "After stressful hours at work, all I need to do is step into the backyard, lie on the hammock, and gaze at the vegetable garden to feel the same peace I felt in my childhood," she says.

picked.t: Sa Pa offers autumn, winter escapes as Vietnam makes Lonely Planet travel list
picked.body: "Fall sees Vietnam in its prime," Lonely Planet wrote in its "Fall Travel Trends 2026: The World's Next 15 Destinations" list. In northern Vietnam, Sa Pa draws visitors with its mountain scenery, cool climate and ethnic cultural traditions. Autumn brings golden rice terraces during the harvest season, while winter offers cloud-covered peaks and, occasionally, frost or snow. One way to take in the scenery is aboard the cable car at Sun World Fansipan Legend, which carries visitors above Muong Hoa Valley, with views of terraced fields, villages and forests. The cable car climbs toward Fansipan, at 3,143 meters above sea level and often called the "Roof of Indochina." On favorable days, visitors can see clouds blanketing the valleys below and mountain peaks rising above the mist. Sunrise and late afternoon can offer particularly striking views, depending on weather conditions. Fansipan also features a spiritual complex with Buddhist statues, temples and mountain pathways. Landmarks include the Amitabha Buddha statue, the Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva statue and the Arhat Path, which winds past old rhododendron trees. After exploring the summit, visitors can stop for drinks at venues such as Du Soleil, Starbucks Fansipan and Phe La, some of which offer mountain views through large windows. At the foot of Fansipan, Ban May Village showcases the cultural traditions of ethnic communities in Vietnam's northwest, including the H'Mong, Xa Pho, Tay, Giay, Red Dao, Thai and Ha Nhi. Visitors can explore traditional architecture and clothing, watch cultural performances and learn crafts such as brocade weaving, incense making, bamboo weaving and beeswax batik. Local cuisine is another part of the Sa Pa experience, particularly as temperatures drop toward the end of the year. Popular dishes include salmon hot pot, charcoal-grilled meats and freshly baked chestnut cakes. As winter sets in, Fansipan may experience frost and, during sufficiently cold spells, snowfall. Snow is uncommon and cannot be guaranteed, but winter often brings dramatic cloud formations around the peaks. From golden terraces and mountain views to traditional crafts and regional food, Sa Pa offers visitors a range of experiences throughout autumn and winter.

picked.t: Struggling taxi driver wins praise for honoring repayment promise after Lexus crash
picked.body: On Oct. 7, Tran Quang Duc of Hanoi’s Vinh Hung Ward received a VND3 million (US$120) transfer from driver Le Giang, along with a message saying: "I still owe you VND4 million, and I will pay the rest next month." The payment stemmed from a collision on Aug. 7, when Duc had parked his Lexus near Noi Bai International Airport while waiting to pick up relatives. Giang’s taxi hit the rear of the vehicle, smashing a taillight and leaving dents and scratches. As the accident happened late at night and Duc’s insurance had expired, he asked Giang for a VND10 million advance and agreed to meet him at a repair shop the next day. Giang borrowed money from relatives and friends and transferred the full amount before leaving. The following morning, a private repair shop on Giai Phong Street estimated the damage at VND50 million. Duc said he chose a private garage rather than an authorized dealership to keep the cost down. Impressed by Giang’s willingness to take responsibility, he decided to cover half the bill himself and asked the driver to pay VND25 million. Giang then raised another VND5 million with help from his wife in Thanh Hoa Province. After learning that he was supporting an ailing wife and three young children, Duc allowed him to pay the remaining VND10 million in installments. "When I suggested installment payments, I mentally wrote the money off because I knew how hard his circumstances were," Duc said. Giang, however, kept his promise. He transferred VND3 million on Sept. 1 and another VND3 million on Oct. 7, each time noting the remaining balance. Duc said he kept the repayment arrangement so Giang could honor his commitment and now plans to return VND10 million to him. "Giving the money back is my way of honoring a decent person who owns up to his mistakes and stands by his word," Duc said. Tran Quang Duc, a resident of Hanoi’s Vinh Hung Ward. Photo courtesy of Duc Giang, 39, is originally from the central province of Thanh Hoa and has worked as a ride-hailing driver in Hanoi for more than a year, earning VND10-15 million a month. As his family’s main breadwinner, he rents a small room in the capital and sets aside part of his monthly income to repay the debt. "I am determined not to break my promise," he said. The story quickly spread on social media, drawing praise for the honesty and compassion shown by the two men.
